1:
Clarke opens by mapping the whole speech: chastity and integrity, then humanity, then charity and mercy, then abhorrence of covetousness and idolatry, and at last the acknowledgment of error and the wish for a full investigation. Ellicott calls it one grand profession of innocence, a rehearsal of Job's manner of life from the first,, who does not content himself with traversing what his friends have charged but professes himself clear of the sins least visible to onlookers, those touching the secret conduct and the heart.

On the covenant itself the witnesses divide over what the eyes were for. Gill reads a solemn engagement made in the strength of divine grace, since the eyes are the inlets to uncleanness; he cites Zaleucus, who had adulterers punished by the plucking out of the eyes, and the poet's figure of beauty passing through the eye swifter than an arrow. Henry presses the bargain further. Job allowed his eyes the light of the sun and the glory of God shining in the visible creation, on condition that they never fasten upon an object which might raise an impure imagination, and under penalty of smarting for it in penitential tears. Those who would keep the heart pure must guard the eyes, he adds, which are at once the outlets and the inlets of uncleanness; the first sin began in the eye. Wesley gives the ground briefly, that Job kept from the least occasions and appearances of evil. Both Henry and Ellicott hear the seventh commandment behind the vow as Christ expounded it, Henry remarking that Job understood it better than the Pharisees who sat in Moses's chair.

Clarke alone takes the verse elsewhere. He renders it "I have cut the covenant sacrifice with my eyes," so that conscience and eyes are the contracting parties and God the judge; and he suspects that the maid is no maid at all. Bethulah, he argues, may here be an idol, on the report of Sanchoniatho that Ouranos first introduced the Baithulia by erecting animated stones, or, as Bochart would have it, anointed ones, each the representative of some deity. These, he supposes, were at first emblems of the house of God, or of the pillar Jacob set up and named, since idolatry always counterfeits a pure worship. Keil and Delitzsch, rendering "how should I fix my gaze upon a maiden," keep the plain sense but mark where Job stands: no Israelite, outside the Sinaitic revelation, holding the old patriarchal religion that Arabs who are not Moslem still call the religion of Abraham, or the religion of the steppe.

The three verses following are Job's reason, and they are read as one question. Gill takes the portion from above to be God himself, the portion of his people in life and at death, and denies it to any who live a vicious course; Clarke turns the question toward Job's own case and asks what reward he has had for not departing. Ellicott makes the third verse simply answer the second, and compares the remonstrance of Joseph. Henry says fools make a mock at this sin and call it a trick of youth, while the destruction of Sodom stands as the strange punishment threatened; he notes the alternative rendering of alienation. On the fourth verse Gill and Clarke agree that no darkness hides the act from an omniscient eye, and Wesley that however secretly the unchaste carry the matter, one stands upon a higher place and sees in what manner they act. Henry takes the counting of steps for the sharper word: God keeps account of every particular step because he will call us to account, and takes more exact notice of us than we do of ourselves, for who ever counted his own steps? Ellicott hears the pronoun as emphatic and the appeal as made to the judge of the hearts and reins.
5:
The vanity Job disclaims is read three ways. Gill offers vain men for company, after Bar Tzemach, or vanity of the mind, but settles on deceitful methods used to cheat and defraud, another vice cleared from the account. Wesley makes it plainer still, lying and falsehood in dealings with men, and finds in the second clause the readiness to grasp an opportunity of enriching oneself by wronging another. Clarke dissents. The word here translated vanity is elsewhere used of a false god, and he holds the whole discourse to be a vindication of Job from every idolatrous disposition and practice.

On the balance the voices agree and differ only in emphasis. Gill renders it balances of righteousness, the strict justice of God, and says Job was so conscious of having done no man injustice that if the rule of righteousness were laid in one scale and his actions in the other the beam would stand even. Clarke glosses the integrity as perfection, the totality of an unblameable life. Wesley takes the clause for an appeal: Job desires nothing more than to have heart and life weighed in just balances and searched out by the all-seeing God, and the words that follow, and he will know, speak of God after the manner of men.

The seventh verse draws the most comment. Ellicott finds the form emphatic and the way meant the narrow one of strict integrity, comparing the name given the first believers, men of the way. Gill takes it for the way of God broadly, and adds a point about Job's dispensation: besides the light of nature which the Gentiles had in common, good men before Moses had some revelation of the mind and will of God, enough to direct them in worship and duty. He does not claim Job never stepped awry, only that he never turned aside knowingly, and never finally persisted when drawn aside by infirmity, by Satan, or by the snares of the world. Keil and Delitzsch read the heart going after the eyes as the heart following the lust of the eye to obtain another man's property by deceit or extortion, and take the blot for a stain, a macula clinging to the hands. Wesley puts it in a line, that sin commonly enters by the eye into the heart, and that the blot is any unjust gain. Clarke declares himself willing to be sifted to the uttermost, for every step of his foot, every thought of his heart, every look of his eye and every act of his hands.

The sentence Job calls down on himself is a farmer's. Gill notes that sowing for another to eat stands among the judgments threatened to the disobedient. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the word for offspring, used elsewhere in the book of children of the body, is here, as in Isaiah, the produce of the ground, and that the line is quoted as a proverb in the fourth Gospel. Wesley reads it of plants, fruits and improvements. Clarke alone attends to the other half of the curse, the rooting out of the offspring, and pauses over it to repeat what he thinks already probable, that not all of Job's children were destroyed in the fall of the house.
9:
Gill guards the first clause against a misreading: the deceiving is not the woman's doing. It comes not by any blame of hers, nor by the artful methods of the harlot in Proverbs, but by a man's own wanton looking; and Job, having covenanted with his eyes, withstood solicitation as Joseph did, though the wisest of men was later drawn aside. Henry sets the matter inward, since all the defilements of the life come from a deceived heart, and every sin is deceitful, none more than this. He adds that Job never laid wait at a neighbour's door for the hour when the good man was out. Clarke notes only that the Septuagint supplies the missing words, another man's wife. Keil and Delitzsch set the paragraph beside the last: having guarded himself against defiling virgin innocence by a glance, Job is conscious of no attempt on a neighbour's marriage either, and the word for neighbour is the Decalogue's own.

The imprecation that follows is the crux. Gill gives both readings and will not choose: some take the grinding literally, of drudgery at a mill, work that fell to women and which Homer speaks of as older than himself; others, with the Targum and Aben Ezra, take it of defilement by another man. Ellicott passes it briefly as menial office, like a slave's. Clarke keeps the handmill, following the Syriac and Arabic, then reads the second clause with unusual candour: to bow down over her is to have no command of her own person, her owner disposing of it at will, since in Asiatic countries slaves were held so absolutely as property that owners lent them to guests. Wesley cautions that Job does not desire this, but that were God to give up his wife to such wickedness he would own the justice of it. Henry answers from providence: God often punishes the sin of one with the sin of another, the husband's adultery with the wife's, as in David's case, which in no way excuses her, since however unrighteous she is, God is righteous.

On the crime and its judges they are nearly of one mind, and reach beyond Job's age to say so. Gill calls it contrary to the light of nature as well as the express law of God, a breach of the marriage covenant, an injury to what is dearest to a man, and the thing that brings confusion into families and states. Wesley points out that the Hebrew has an iniquity of the judges, theirs to punish with death, not by the law of Moses only but by the law of nature, as the customs of the heathen nations show. Henry presses it home to the speaker: so it was adjudged in the patriarchal age, before the law of Moses made it capital, and it is to be punished though the guilty man be himself a judge, as Job was. Clarke reports Mr. Good's rendering, a premeditated crime and a profligacy of the understanding, and holds the offence against society and not the parties only.

The fire at the end is read at four depths. Gill offers them in order: the burning of the lust itself; the unappeasable rage of jealousy in the injured man; the punishment practised by the Gentiles of Job's neighbourhood, who burned such offenders; or, as he prefers, the wrath of God itself. Clarke keeps to the house, where nothing is so destructive of peace, jealousy brings unmixed misery, and the offender wastes his substance on the objects of an impure affection. Henry and Wesley take it inward and then upward together: lust is a fire in the soul which eats the convictions and the comforts, lays the conscience waste, wastes body and substance, and kindles a divine wrath which, unless quenched by the blood of Christ, burns to the lowest hell. Henry suspects an allusion to the burning of Sodom.
13:
Ellicott identifies the charge being answered. Eliphaz had insinuated that Job favoured the rich and powerful while grinding down the weak, and Job meets it by claiming that he regarded his own servants as brethren, partakers of a common humanity. Gill spells out what the cause could be. If it were a quarrel between two of them brought before him, he did not reject it for the meanness of the parties or the servitude they stood in, but heard each patiently, examined the merits, and either reconciled them or passed sentence, punishing the delinquent and protecting the innocent; if it were a complaint against himself, of work, wages, food or clothing, he heard that too.

Clarke supplies the legal background that makes the claim remarkable. In ancient times slaves had no action at law against their owners, who might dispose of them as of cattle or any other property; a slave might complain and an owner might listen if he chose, but he was not compelled to. Job, he says, admitted his servants to all civil rights, and so far from shutting out their case was ready to let them complain against himself and to give them the whole benefit of the law.

The reason Job gives runs in two directions, and the witnesses follow both. Looking forward, Gill has him at an utter loss for an excuse when God rises up to defend the injured, whether in providence now or at the great day, when masters and servants stand alike before the judgment seat to receive for the things they have done. Clarke says the same in the first person: at that bar king and subject, master and slave are on an equal footing, every civil distinction abolished for ever, and he cannot see how he should stand there had he dealt unjustly, since he has treated others as he wished to be treated.

Looking back to the womb, Gill observes that though parents are the instruments of begetting, God is the maker of men, and all are fabricated in the same shop of nature. Keil and Delitzsch put the argument formally: the same manner of birth, by the same divine creative power and the same human agency, makes master and servant substantially brethren with equal claims. They also weigh the disputed word. Taken as a noun it means God, the One, as in Malachi, and so the Targum, the Vulgate, Saadia and Gecatilia read it; the Septuagint, the Syriac and Symmachus instead attach it as an adjective to the womb, and the accentuation agrees with them. Against the first reading it has been objected that the word would want the article, which they answer was not absolutely necessary. Ellicott, more briefly, hears the verse again as a reply to Eliphaz.
16:
Henry names the charge rebutted. Eliphaz had said outright that Job withheld bread from the hungry, stripped the naked and sent widows away empty; Wesley notes that Job is longest here because here he was most accused. Gill keeps the claim modest: the desires withheld would be reasonable ones within his power, not the unbounded requests the sons of Zebedee made. Henry reads the widow's failing eyes as a look and not a petition, in one without confidence enough to ask; and he has the fatherless eat with Job rather than after him, off the same dish, since the sharpest grievance of poverty is the contempt it draws.

Clarke sets the morsel in the ancient custom of the table, where supper was the meal of fellowship and friends and strangers alike were welcome; a man is a despicable caitiff, he says, who eats alone with another at hand as hungry. On the verse following he gives up. He lays the renderings side by side: Heath takes the two pronouns of a male and a female orphan, Houbigant and the Vulgate make commiseration itself the nurse that reared Job, Coverdale has mercy growing up with him, the Septuagint and Syriac have him nourish the poor as a father, the Arabic has him schooled in distresses and groans. Who, he asks, can reconcile translations so discordant? Ellicott and Wesley cut the knot by referring the pronouns to the fatherless and the widow already named; Gill and Henry read the line biographically, that Job began this as soon as he could tell good from evil.

Gill will not let the seeing of the next verse stand neutral: one version has it despising and another overlooking, and Job denies both, not that he never saw such a case but that he never saw one and passed by. Henry observes that covering costs more than feeding: instead of rich liveries for the servants while the poor went off in rags, Job had warm strong garments made from the fleece of his own sheep. Those sheep were afterwards burned with fire from heaven, and Henry locates the comfort exactly there, that while he had them he came by them honestly and used them charitably. Clarke calls the blessing of the loins a delicate touch, the shivering part now covered in warm woollen and by a fine prosopopoeia made to bless its clothier.

The lifted hand Gill unpacks into its possible acts: a threat, terrifying to the poor when a magistrate makes it; a blow; a signal to others to strike, as Ananias gave order against Paul; or a vote cast wrongly, suffrages being sometimes taken by the lifting of hands. Henry and Wesley both fix on the reason attached, that Job saw his help in the gate and could have influenced the judges to do as he pleased. Clarke leaves the text to print Lebid from the Moallakat in Sir William Jones's version, for its portrait of a bountiful chief who divides the slaughtered camel by lot and relinquishes his own right to establish his people's.

The imprecation is anatomical. Gill takes it at full weight, the arm disjointed or rotting off, and recalls Jeroboam's withering when he stretched it out against the prophet; since Eliphaz had charged that the arms of the fatherless were broken, Job asks for his own on the same terms. Such oaths, Gill warns, suit only a case where innocence cannot otherwise be cleared. Clarke, citing Good, would have judgment fall on the parts that did the wrong. What restrained Job was not men but God. Gill says he feared no man, having them at his command; Henry makes it awe at the infinite distance, since one higher than the highest regards. Ellicott corrects the last clause to say Job was unable to act thus, and Wesley that he could neither oppose that power nor bear that wrath.
24:
Ellicott ties the turn to gold back to an admonition of Eliphaz, which Job denies was his practice. Gill treats the paragraph as the figurative half of a charge of idolatry, the literal half coming after: covetousness is idolatry, since to make gold the ground of hope puts it in the room of the Hope of Israel, and true hope is of things unseen and to come. Henry states the principle plainly: wealth is advantageous or pernicious according to how we stand affected to it, our ruin if we make it our rest and ruler, a blessing if we make it our servant. It is hard, he adds, to have riches and not trust in riches, which is why the rich man enters the kingdom with such difficulty.

Gill leaves a lawful joy standing: a man may rejoice in the God who has increased his substance and made him able to do good, and what Job denies is the carnal joy that engrosses the affections. Henry hears the real disclaimer in the second clause, that his hand had gotten it, and says Job's joy never terminated in the gift but passed through to the giver. He then makes the point that carries the whole book: the way to weep as though we wept not is to rejoice as though we rejoiced not, and the less pleasure taken in the enjoyment, the less pain in the loss. That, he thinks, is how Job bore his so patiently.

The sun and moon divide them more than anything else here. Gill lists four readings before choosing: that the changeableness of sun and moon proves earthly things uncertain; that Job denies, with Nachmanides, ascribing his substance to their influence; that he still speaks of his own prosperity; or, with Schultens, that he means the flattery of great personages. Gill takes it literally all the same. Clarke names the thing: Sabaeism, the most ancient and most reasonable of all species of idolatry, and sets out from Calmet its three parts, the worship of sun and moon, the adoring of the sun at its rising and the moon at her change, and the kissing of the hand. Ellicott finds it remarkable that this is the only idolatry Job repudiates, as though ignorant of the grosser kinds; Wesley agrees that the host of heaven was the oldest idolatry, and commonest in the East.

The gesture draws close attention. Keil and Delitzsch explain that a kiss is a joining of lip to lip, so the hand a man kisses may equally be said to kiss his mouth; turning it toward the object of veneration is the proper act of adoration,; they cite Pliny for the right hand carried to the kiss while the body turns about, and Tacitus for the Syrians venerating the rising sun. Henry keeps it homely: those who could not reach the sun as the sacrificers kissed the calves paid this compliment instead, reverencing as masters what God made servants to hold the candle for us. Gill locates the sin earlier, in a heart drawn by the magnitude of those bodies and the swiftness of their motion to think them divine, for there is a secret idolatry as well as a secret worship of the true God.

The closing verse divides them over the judge. Wesley and Gill take him for the civil magistrate, advanced by God and bound to vindicate his honour; Gill notes that the law of Moses made the offence capital and that the Targum calls it a most amazing iniquity. Ellicott prefers my judge, meaning God, and doubts any reference to the Mosaic law here. On the denial all agree with Clarke, that to adore the lights would be to deny the God who made them; Henry presses furthest, calling idolatry in effect atheism, and a public nuisance too, since it debauches manners and unties the bond of societies.
29:
Ellicott marks the change of ground. Job now passes into the realm of wishes and thoughts, and is, he says, far more thorough and searching with his own case than his friends had been with it. Gill takes the enmity as a given: Job had enemies, as good men have, and precisely on account of their goodness, there being a rooted bitterness in the seed of the serpent against the godly in every generation. Destruction comes on such men sooner or later, in their families, their bodies or their substance, and it is common enough for the wicked to be glad of it. What Job disclaims, Gill says, is not the act but the feeling, and he concedes how hard that is: it takes a large measure of grace in exercise not to feel a secret pleasure at the news of a calamity falling on an enemy. Clarke puts the same denial flatly, that he neither avenged himself nor bore malice or hatred.

The tongue is treated as the next stage down. Gill observes that the mouth, being the instrument of speech, is often the instrument of much sin, and of cursing above all; Job laid an embargo on his, keeping it as with a bridle, so that not even his worst adversary had an evil wish uttered against him. Clarke turns it on the reader: he neither spoke evil of his enemy nor wished him evil, and how few of those called Christians can say as much of people who have done them mischief.

The verse about the men of the tent is the hardest in the passage, and the witnesses divide over what the household was saying. Clarke thinks the Targum gives the best sense, that they asked who had ever ordered them to go unsatisfied with his flesh; that is, his servants lived like his own children and were served from the same dishes as his family, and never saw meat come to his table while they were put off with pulse. Good's rendering points the same way, asking where the man is who went hungry for his meat. Keil and Delitzsch read it so too, taking the people of the tent for all who belonged to it, chiefly the servants though not to the exclusion of wife, children and kindred, and denying that the flesh in question is any person's. Ellicott and Wesley take it the other way, as the cry of retainers so hot in their master's quarrel that they swore they could eat his enemy's flesh and never have enough; on that reading the point of the verse is that Job held both them and himself back from the revenge they were pressing on him.

Hospitality closes the list. Gill is careful about the word: the stranger here is not the man estranged from God, nor the pilgrim on earth, but simply one out of his own country, good or bad alike, whom Job would not leave lying in the street at night under the weather. Clarke widens it past the household, since the perfectly unknown man and the traveller bound for some other district both found his doors open and were refreshed with his bed and his board. Ellicott hears behind the verse the manners of Genesis and Judges, if not the incidents recorded there, and notes that the word rendered traveller is literally the road, so that the man meant is the wayfarer upon it.
33:
Gill opens by saying what the chapter does not claim. Nothing in this account of a holy life means Job thought himself free from sin; he has owned himself a sinner already and disclaimed perfection, and speaks here of transgressions in the plural. What he denies is the covering. Adam covered his by laying the blame on his wife, and she hers on the serpent, and those excuses, Gill says, were inventions the pair found out for themselves. Clarke finds the allusion unmistakable and counts three concealments in Genesis: Adam hid among the trees, then charged the woman, then charged God with having given her to him. He thinks Job refers directly to the Mosaic account, and reads the verse to mean that whenever Job departed from rectitude he acknowledged the error and sought no palliative. Wesley agrees in four words, as Adam did in Paradise.

Ellicott will not have it settled so quickly. The phrase may equally mean as man commonly does, and he judges that there may or may not be any indication here of acquaintance with the narrative of Genesis. Gill, who prefers the Adam reading, concedes the other as a second sense: Job did not do as men commonly do, concealing sin through fear or shame, unless they are such hardened sinners as the men of Sodom. Henry supplies the accusation being answered, that Zophar had insinuated Job hid his iniquity under his tongue. He never made fig leaves the shelter of his shame, Henry says, nor kept his iniquity in his bosom as a darling he could not part with, nor as stolen goods whose discovery he dreaded; covering sins is natural to us because we have it from our first parents, and he who covers them shall not prosper. The protestation proves two things on Henry's account: that Job had no great concealed iniquity, and that such faults as he had, since no man lives and sins not, he was ready to unsay and undo by confession to God and men.

The second verse gives the motive a man might have for such hiding, and Keil and Delitzsch state it exactly: Job was neither an open sinner nor, out of fear of men and a feeling of honour, a secret one. What he might have dreaded was the moral judgment of the people and the stigma attaching to families, the loss of standing in the higher circles, whose consequence would be a man keeping quiet and retired and never going out of his door. Gill takes the same words of confession rather than of sin, that no multitude ever deterred him from acknowledging a fault publicly when a public acknowledgment was called for.

Henry and Wesley read the line as a claim to courage and make it the evidence of sincerity. Job was a man of undaunted resolution in a good cause, who appeared, spoke and acted for religion and justice and was never browbeaten out of his duty. Henry presses the corollary, that silence and retirement may themselves be the sin, as when a man is called to reprove wickedness or do justice to the oppressed; Job valued neither the clamours of the multitude nor the menaces of the mighty, fearing the great God rather than the crowd, and his curse rather than the contempt of families. Clarke asks the question in his own terms, whether the voice of the many ever kept him from decreeing what was right, or whether he was ever constrained to keep his house rather than give judgment against his conscience. He then reports Good, who takes the verse the other way round, not as a question at all but as a curse Job calls down on himself: let him be confounded before the assembled multitude, let the reproach of its families quash him, let him be struck dumb and never appear abroad.
35:
The whole passage is courtroom language, and the witnesses read it as a formal motion. Gill renders the opening, who will give me a hearer, and specifies the sort wanted: not a hearer of the kind Job once had as a teacher of many, nor an idler who comes into court out of curiosity, but one who will hear him plead judicially. Keil and Delitzsch narrow it. The wish is put generally, but since the case turns on a contradiction between outward appearance and veiled fact, the only competent hearer is the searcher of hearts, and the clause following is not a wish but an assertion, that the Almighty will answer. Henry keeps the wider sense and draws the moral: an upright heart does not dread a scrutiny, and a man who means honestly could wish he had a window in his breast.

The next clause turns on a technical word. Clarke reads it as a pledge entered, Job binding himself under a great penalty to appear and abide the issue; Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering, here is my mark, that is, the signature Job is ready to subscribe. Both want the adversary's charge reduced to writing rather than left vague, and Ellicott would render the wish as having the indictment in hand, in black and white, to be answered point by point. Wesley draws an inference from the request: the charge was to be given in a book or paper, as the manner was in judicial proceedings, and this shows that Job did not live before letters were in use. Henry gives three reasons for wanting such a document: if it showed a sin he had not seen, he would be glad to know it and repent; if it charged what was false, he did not doubt he could disprove it; and he suspected that once his accusers had to write the thing down, the charges would prove trivial.

What Job says he would do with the indictment is the striking part. Gill offers three senses: that he would carry it as a light thing having no real weight of guilt in it, or confess openly whatever it proved, or, as he prefers, bear it not as a burden but as an honour, the way a man carries a sword of state on his shoulder. Clarke illustrates from a book of Chinese punishments before him, in which the accused carry a board with the charge written on it, sometimes a heavy plank pierced for the neck like a pillory and worn for months; Job would carry such a thing between accusation and judgment and, far from counting it a disgrace, would bind it on as a diadem, as an eastern man puts a gift from a superior straight upon his head.

On the last verse the commentators split over the bearing Job means to take. Gill has him forwarding the case against himself, furnishing materials and giving an account of every transaction he can remember, not because God needs the information but to show that he does not fear the closest examination. Clarke has him laying out the stations and offices of his life, civil, military and domestic, and going in as the sovereign commander who will not shrink from investigation by the meanest of his subjects. Ellicott reports both readings and declines to choose: either Job would give the account with alacrity and perfect confidence, or he would approach as one approaches a prince, with the utmost deference, not as an enemy but as one worthy of honour; the actual meaning, he says, is uncertain. Wesley takes the first, with undaunted courage. Ellicott also observes that the order here is out of sequence, these verses belonging properly after the three that close the chapter, and he puts that down to the writer's ideas of symmetry not being ours.
38:
The commentators argue over where these verses belong. Clarke says the most careless reader may see that they disturb the connection and are evidently out of place; Gill reports that some would put them after the twenty-fifth verse, but observes that this is their order in all copies and versions, and defends it: Job, having asked for a hearing and for his charge in writing, returns to clear himself of one last thing, and having done with his private life ends with his public. That last charge, Gill says, is tyranny and oppression, laid on him by his friends without proof.

The crying land is read two ways. Wesley takes it of title, the ground crying because it was got by fraud, and Gill allows that sense first. Clarke takes it of husbandry, referring the verse to the sabbatical law by which land rested every seventh year so the soil should not be exhausted, in a country with few means of improving arable ground by manure; Job's fields could not complain, having neither broken that law nor been worn out. Gill allows this second sense too. Ellicott attends to the figure rather than the charge, rendering the second clause that the furrows weep together and calling it a strong impersonation for the consequence of wrong-doing. Henry says the whole creation groans under man's sin, but what is unjustly gained cries out against its holder, so that the furrows become his prosecutors.

On the next verse the witnesses distinguish two sorts of theft. Gill takes eating the fruits without money of a man who got his land from its rightful owners by deceit, left his ploughmen unpaid, or took his tenants' produce without a proper price. Clarke adds another: the narrow-minded man who through covetousness exhausts his ground, at no charge for labour or manure, has eaten its fruits without money as truly as the defrauder; and Coverdale, he notes, renders the second clause as grieving any of the ploughmen. Wesley and Henry take the last clause at its worst and name the precedent, a man killing the owner for undisturbed possession, as Ahab did with Naboth; Henry sets against it Abraham paying for the field he bought.

The closing curse turns on two obscure plants. Gill glosses them as thistles for wheat and, for barley, cockle or darnel or any stinking weed, and hears behind the imprecation the original curse upon the earth, a fruitful land turned to barrenness for the wickedness of those who dwell in it. Clarke works at the words: the first may be a hooked thorn, the second a fetid plant, rendered wild grapes elsewhere, taken by Bishop Lowth for poisonous berries, by Hasselquist for the hoary nightshade of Egypt and Palestine, and by others for the aconite. Henry draws the moral, that men who get estates unjustly are justly deprived of the comfort of them: it was sown wheat and shall come up thistles.

The last sentence is itself disputed. Clarke doubts it belongs to the book at all: it is wanting in many Vulgate manuscripts, including two of his own and the first printed edition, and he supposes a scribe wrote it in rubric and a later hand took it into the text. In the Hebrew, he adds, the lines are complete without it. Keil and Delitzsch render it with the rest. Henry takes it for the true close of the defence, all Job means to say to his friends, though he speaks again afterwards in self-reproach; the manner carries an air of assurance, as of a man who keeps the field, yet Henry cautions that, confident as Job was, he would be shown mistaken. Ellicott sums up the chapter as more than a traverse of the indictment: Job has shown himself not merely unbroken in the moral law but exemplary in every relation of life.
